# Kukkuravatika Sutta (MN 57 (PTS MN i 387))
**ID:** MN 57 (PTS MN i 387)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kukkuravatika Sutta* ("The Ascetic Who Behaved Like a Dog", MN 57) is the fifty-seventh discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. In this discourse, the Buddha encounters two ascetics undertaking imitation of animal practices: Puṇṇa, who practices bovine vows (imitating an ox or cow), and the naked ascetic Seniya, who follows a canine discipline (*kukkurasīla*, *kukkuravata*) by acting like a dog [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Gombrich 1996; Rogell 2003]. When pressed to reveal their future destiny, the Buddha explains that fully cultivating such mental inclinations (*saṅkhāra*) and habits leads inevitably to rebirth as a dog or an ox, whereas entertaining the mistaken view that such vows lead to purification or heaven causes rebirth in hell [Moult; Argumentation 2008; Bodhi 2003; Evans; Anālayo 2010; Gombrich 1996]. The text thus serves as an explicit critique of extreme ascetic austerities and clinging to rules and vows (*sīlabbatupādāna*) [Bodhi 2003; Carpenter 2014; von Hinüber 1996].
The sutta is doctrinally notable for articulating a fourfold classification of karma based on the polarity of dark (*kaṇha*) and bright (*sukka*): (1) dark action with dark result, (2) bright action with bright result, (3) dark and bright action with mixed result, and (4) action that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, which constitutes the action leading to the cessation or destruction of karma [Argumentation 2008; Powers 2016; Rogell 2003]. Modern philosophical studies observe that this schema was designed to be exhaustive, categorizing saṃsāric merit (*puñña*) and demerit (*apuñña*), while placing the conduct and wholesome states (*dhamma*) of the liberated person (*arahant*) beyond the fruit-bearing cycle of karmic maturation [Argumentation 2008; Finnigan].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include *Catukkanipāta* discourses (AN 4.232 and AN 4.233), the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), and a Chinese counterpart in the *Abhidharmasaṅgītiparyāyapāda* (T 1536.5); the sutta is also cited in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) and *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 14.8, Kv 15.11) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies 1,542 Pali-internal matches across 108 texts, confirming substantial textual overlap with the *Catukkanipāta* (especially §7.1–8.5 with AN 4.233 §233.1.1–233.2.5), AN 3 (§10.2–10.6), SN 42 (§11.4–12.4), and Kv 15.11 (§10.2–10.9) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the discourse with Tibetan translations—most notably the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* (D4054), and *Vinayavastu* (D0001)—as well as Chinese collections including the *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) and *Ekottarika Āgama* (T 125) [DharmaNexus].
